title: Physics Midterm — Definitions, Constants, Formulas & Original 83 Problems
subject: Physics
description: Worksheet-aligned Physics flashcards: exact rounding rules, definitions, standard values, formula selection and all 83 original assigned problems. No generic study-strategy questions.

cards.front: For measured ADDITION (+), round based on what?
cards.back: Fewest DECIMAL PLACES. Example: 8.9435 + 79.86 = 88.80.

cards.front: For measured SUBTRACTION (−), round based on what?
cards.back: Fewest DECIMAL PLACES. Example: 35.864 − 7.2 = 28.7.

cards.front: For measured MULTIPLICATION (×), round based on what?
cards.back: Fewest SIGNIFICANT FIGURES. Example: 4.241 × 6.4 = 27 (2 sig figs).

cards.front: For measured DIVISION (÷), round based on what?
cards.back: Fewest SIGNIFICANT FIGURES. Example: 83.6364 ÷ 83.6 = 1.00 (3 sig figs).

cards.front: 35.864 minus 7.2: which precision rule controls the result?
cards.back: Subtraction → decimal PLACES. 7.2 has 1 decimal place; 28.664 becomes 28.7.

cards.front: 4.241 times 6.4: which precision rule controls the result?
cards.back: Multiplication → significant FIGURES. 6.4 has 2 significant figures; 27.1424 becomes 27.

cards.front: Which has three significant figures: 0.00450 or 0.0045?
cards.back: 0.00450 has 3 significant figures (4, 5, trailing 0); 0.0045 has 2.

cards.front: For measured 12.11 plus 0.3, how many decimal places?
cards.back: One decimal place. The exact sum is 12.41, reported as 12.4.

cards.front: For measured 3.14 times 2.0, how many significant figures?
cards.back: Two significant figures. The product is 6.28, reported as 6.3.

cards.front: For measured addition or subtraction, how should you round?
cards.back: To the fewest decimal places among the measured inputs.

cards.front: For measured multiplication or division, how should you round?
cards.back: To the fewest significant figures among measured inputs.

cards.front: Do leading zeros count as significant figures?
cards.back: No. They only position the decimal point.

cards.front: Do zeros between nonzero digits count as significant?
cards.back: Yes. These are called captive zeros.

cards.front: Do trailing zeros after a decimal point count as significant?
cards.back: Yes. They communicate measurement precision.

cards.front: Why can a whole number ending in zeros be ambiguous?
cards.back: Without notation, it may not show which trailing zeros were measured.

cards.front: How can scientific notation clarify significant figures?
cards.back: It explicitly displays the measured digits in the coefficient.

cards.front: Do exact counts limit significant-figure precision?
cards.back: No. Exact counts and exact unit definitions do not limit precision.

cards.front: Why is 4.241 × 6.4 rounded to 27, not 27.1424?
cards.back: 6.4 has only 2 significant figures. Products are reported to the fewest sig figs.

cards.front: For a calculation combining + and ×, which precision rule applies?
cards.back: Apply decimal-place limits at +/− steps and sig-fig limits at ×/÷ steps. Avoid early rounding.

cards.front: What rounding rule applies to mixed operations?
cards.back: Apply the rule for each operation; retain guard digits until the final report.

cards.front: What happens when the input numbers are exact counts?
cards.back: Exact counts do not restrict significant figures; measured values still determine the reported precision.

cards.front: What is the purpose of dimensional analysis?
cards.back: Change units systematically by multiplying by equivalent ratios.

cards.front: What is a conversion factor?
cards.back: A ratio of equivalent quantities that equals 1.

cards.front: Where should the unwanted unit appear in a conversion fraction?
cards.back: Opposite its position in the original quantity, so it cancels.

cards.front: What exact relation connects kilometers and meters?
What exact relation connects meters and centimeters?
What exact relation connects hours and seconds?
What exact relation connects inches and centimeters?
What exact relation connects liters and cubic centimeters?
What exact relation connects feet and inches?
cards.back: 1 ft = 12 in.

cards.front: What is the formula for average speed?
cards.back: Speed = total distance traveled ÷ elapsed time.

cards.front: What is the definition of density?
cards.back: Mass divided by volume, often expressed in kg/m³ or g/cm³.

cards.front: How do you convert an area unit?
cards.back: Square the entire length conversion factor.

cards.front: How do you convert a volume unit?
cards.back: Cube the entire length conversion factor.

cards.front: Why is 1 m² equal to 10,000 cm²?
cards.back: Because (100 cm / 1 m)² = 10,000 cm²/m².

cards.front: When converting acceleration to another time unit, what must change?
cards.back: The squared time conversion as well as the distance unit.

cards.front: For an echo problem, why double the distance to a cliff?
cards.back: Sound travels to the cliff and returns before it is heard.

cards.front: Is sound speed in air a fixed universal number?
cards.back: No. It varies with conditions, notably temperature.

cards.front: About how fast is sound in air at 20°C?
cards.back: About 343 m/s; this is a temperature-dependent approximation.

cards.front: What is the exact length of 1 mile in feet?
cards.back: 1 mile = 5,280 feet (exact).

cards.front: What is the exact length of 1 mile in meters?
cards.back: 1 international mile = 1,609.344 meters (exact).

cards.front: What is the exact conversion from hours to minutes?
cards.back: 1 hour = 60 minutes (exact).

cards.front: What is the exact conversion from minutes to seconds?
cards.back: 1 minute = 60 seconds (exact).

cards.front: What is the exact conversion from kilograms to grams?
cards.back: 1 kilogram = 1,000 grams (exact).

cards.front: What is the exact conversion from grams to milligrams?
cards.back: 1 gram = 1,000 milligrams (exact).

cards.front: What is 1 cubic meter in liters?
cards.back: 1 m³ = 1,000 L (exact).

cards.front: What is 1 meter squared in square centimeters?
cards.back: 1 m² = 10,000 cm²; square the 100-to-1 linear conversion.

cards.front: What is 1 meter cubed in cubic centimeters?
cards.back: 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³; cube the 100-to-1 linear conversion.

cards.front: In the guide, how many grams equal one carat?
cards.back: 1 carat = 0.2 grams (exact metric carat definition).

cards.front: What approximate speed of sound does the echo problem use?
cards.back: 343 m/s for air near 20°C; estimated, temperature-dependent, not universal.

cards.front: A worksheet says “convert mi/h to m/s.” What method should you choose?
cards.back: Dimensional analysis. Multiply by length and time conversion factors, orienting each so unwanted units cancel.

cards.front: A worksheet says “convert m² to cm².” What must be squared?
cards.back: Square the full length conversion: (100 cm / 1 m)².

cards.front: A worksheet says “convert inches cubed to centimeters cubed.” What method?
cards.back: Cube the linear factor: (2.54 cm / 1 in)³.

cards.front: A worksheet says “convert g/cm³ to kg/m³.” What method?
cards.back: Change mass numerator and cubic-length denominator separately; use 1 kg = 1,000 g and 1 m = 100 cm.

cards.front: A worksheet asks for distance per time. Which relationship?
cards.back: Average speed = total distance ÷ elapsed time; d is distance and t is elapsed time.

cards.front: An echo returns from a cliff. Which distance belongs in the time formula?
cards.back: The round-trip distance: 2 × the one-way distance. Time = total distance ÷ sound speed.

cards.front: What must you do when changing m/s² to km/h²?
cards.back: Convert length from meters to kilometers AND square the seconds-to-hours conversion factor.

cards.front: A worksheet asks for density. What equation applies?
cards.back: ρ = m/V; ρ is density, m is mass, V is volume. Use mass/volume units such as kg/m³.

cards.front: What distinguishes a vector from a scalar?
cards.back: A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only.

cards.front: What is displacement?
cards.back: The directed change from starting position to final position.

cards.front: Is total distance traveled always equal to displacement magnitude?
cards.back: No. A changing path may be longer than the straight-line displacement.

cards.front: How can perpendicular vector components be combined?
cards.back: Magnitude R = √(x² + y²), for perpendicular x and y.

cards.front: What does θ represent in a vector calculation?
cards.back: An angle measured from a specified reference axis, usually in degrees.

cards.front: When an angle is measured from the +x axis, what is x?
cards.back: x = R cos θ, with direction determining the sign.

cards.front: When an angle is measured from the +x axis, what is y?
cards.back: y = R sin θ, with direction determining the sign.

cards.front: What does SOH mean?
cards.back: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse.

cards.front: What does CAH mean?
cards.back: cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse.

cards.front: What does TOA mean?
cards.back: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.

cards.front: What is the hypotenuse of a right triangle?
cards.back: The side opposite the 90° angle; the triangle’s longest side.

cards.front: What does inverse tangent calculate?
cards.back: An angle from a known opposite-to-adjacent side ratio.

cards.front: What calculator setting is used for angles in this course?
cards.back: Degrees (DEG), not radians.

cards.front: Why check the quadrant when finding a vector direction?
cards.back: The signs of x and y determine the correct direction.

cards.front: How should you add two angled vectors?
cards.back: Resolve each into x and y components, add like components, then find result.

cards.front: When should the Pythagorean theorem NOT be used directly?
cards.back: When components are not perpendicular.

cards.front: A hiker walks east, then north. Need straight-line displacement. Which formula?
cards.back: R = √(x²+y²) if x and y are perpendicular components; R is displacement magnitude.

cards.front: Two perpendicular components are known; direction is requested. Which formula?
cards.back: θ = tan⁻¹(y/x), check the quadrant (or use atan2). θ is the direction angle.

cards.front: An angled vector’s size and angle from horizontal are given. Find horizontal part?
cards.back: x = R cos θ; R is magnitude, θ is angle from +x, x is the horizontal component.

cards.front: An angled vector’s size and angle from horizontal are given. Find vertical part?
cards.back: y = R sin θ; R is magnitude, θ is angle from +x, y is the vertical component.

cards.front: A right triangle gives rise and hypotenuse. Which inverse trig finds an angle?
cards.back: θ = sin⁻¹(opposite/hypotenuse), using degree mode if the angle is in degrees.

cards.front: A right triangle gives run and hypotenuse. Which inverse trig finds an angle?
cards.back: θ = cos⁻¹(adjacent/hypotenuse), using degree mode.

cards.front: Two vectors are not at right angles. How do you add them?
cards.back: Find each vector’s signed x/y components, add x values and y values, then calculate resultant magnitude and angle.

cards.front: In a vector diagram, is west positive or negative x?
cards.back: Usually west is negative x and east positive x, if that coordinate convention is chosen.

cards.front: What does kinematics describe?
cards.back: Motion, such as displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time.

cards.front: What unit is used for velocity?
cards.back: Meters per second (m/s) in SI.

cards.front: What unit is used for acceleration?
cards.back: Meters per second squared (m/s²) in SI.

cards.front: What does acceleration measure?
cards.back: Change in velocity per second; SI unit m/s².

cards.front: Under constant acceleration, how is final velocity calculated?
cards.back: v_f = v_i + a t.

cards.front: Under constant acceleration, how is displacement calculated from time?
cards.back: Δx = v_i t + ½ a t².

cards.front: Which constant-acceleration equation omits time?
cards.back: v_f² = v_i² + 2 a Δx.

cards.front: When do constant-acceleration equations apply?
cards.back: When acceleration is constant over the interval.

cards.front: In ideal projectile motion, what happens to horizontal velocity?
cards.back: It stays constant when air resistance is neglected.

cards.front: In ideal projectile motion, what changes vertical velocity?
cards.back: Gravity, approximated as 9.8 m/s² downward near Earth.

cards.front: How is horizontal launch velocity split into components?
cards.back: v₀x = v₀ cos θ and v₀y = v₀ sin θ, for angle from horizontal.

cards.front: With upward positive, what is vertical displacement of a projectile?
cards.back: Δy = v₀y t − ½ g t²; ignore drag.

cards.front: With upward positive, what is vertical projectile velocity?
cards.back: v_y = v₀y − g t; ignore drag.

cards.front: At the highest point of a projectile, what is its vertical velocity?
cards.back: Momentarily zero, although gravity still accelerates it downward.

cards.front: When does t_flight = 2 v₀y/g apply?
cards.back: Only if launch and landing heights are equal, without air drag.

cards.front: What is the free-fall time from rest through height h?
cards.back: t = √(2h/g), assuming constant downward g and no drag.

cards.front: How can the speed from perpendicular velocity parts be found?
cards.back: |v| = √(v_x² + v_y²).

cards.front: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
cards.back: Speed is scalar; velocity includes direction.

cards.front: Known initial speed, acceleration, and time; asked final speed. Which formula?
cards.back: v_f = v_i + at. v_f/v_i: velocities (m/s); a: constant acceleration (m/s²); t: time (s).

cards.front: Known initial velocity, time and acceleration; asked displacement. Which formula?
cards.back: Δx = v_i t + ½at². Δx: displacement (m); v_i: initial velocity (m/s); a: constant acceleration (m/s²).

cards.front: Initial/final speeds and displacement are involved, but time is absent. Which formula?
cards.back: v_f² = v_i² + 2aΔx. v: velocity (m/s), a: constant acceleration (m/s²), Δx: displacement (m).

cards.front: A ball is dropped from rest through height h. Which time formula?
cards.back: t = √(2h/g): h = falling distance (m), g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward; only for constant g and negligible drag.

cards.front: A projectile is launched horizontally. How do you find horizontal distance?
cards.back: Δx = v₀x t; v₀x is horizontal velocity (m/s), t is elapsed time (s); assume no drag.

cards.front: An angled projectile is launched and time t is known. Which vertical position formula?
cards.back: Δy = v₀y t − ½gt². Δy: vertical displacement; v₀y: initial vertical speed; g: gravity, up is positive.

cards.front: Need vertical speed of a projectile at a certain time. Which formula?
cards.back: v_y = v₀y − gt. v_y: vertical velocity (m/s); v₀y: initial vertical velocity; g: gravity.

cards.front: Need horizontal and vertical launch speed from total speed and angle. Which formulas?
cards.back: v₀x = v₀ cosθ; v₀y = v₀ sinθ. v₀ is launch speed, θ angle from horizontal.

cards.front: A projectile lands at the same height it launched. Find total flight time?
cards.back: t = 2v₀y/g. v₀y is initial vertical velocity (m/s), g downward acceleration; equal heights and no drag.

cards.front: A projectile lands at a different height from launch. Can 2v₀y/g be used?
cards.back: No. Solve Δy = v₀y t − ½gt² using the actual height change.

cards.front: Does zero vertical speed at the top of a flight mean zero acceleration?
cards.back: No. At the top, vertical velocity is momentarily zero but acceleration remains g downward.

cards.front: A projectile has v_x and v_y at impact. How do you find total speed?
cards.back: |v| = √(v_x²+v_y²), because horizontal and vertical velocity components are perpendicular.

cards.front: What is a common near-Earth approximation for g?
cards.back: 9.8 m/s² downward, near Earth’s surface.

cards.front: Is g = 9.8 m/s² an exact universal constant?
cards.back: No. It is a near-Earth approximation; use a stated problem value if given.

cards.front: What exact SI unit relation defines a newton?
cards.back: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

cards.front: What does Newton’s second law state?
cards.back: Net force ΣF = m a, using consistent units.

cards.front: What is net force?
cards.back: The vector sum of all real forces on an object.

cards.front: When is net force zero?
cards.back: When acceleration is zero: at rest or moving at constant velocity.

cards.front: What is weight near Earth?
cards.back: Weight = m g, a downward force in newtons.

cards.front: Is mass the same physical quantity as weight?
cards.back: No. Mass is measured in kg; weight is gravitational force in N.

cards.front: What is the normal force N?
cards.back: The force from a surface perpendicular to it; measured in newtons (N).

cards.front: Can normal force differ from mg?
cards.back: Yes, on slopes or when additional vertical forces or acceleration exist.

cards.front: What is kinetic friction for a sliding object?
cards.back: f_k = μ_k N, where μ_k is unitless and N is the normal force.

cards.front: In which direction does kinetic friction act?
cards.back: Opposite the relative sliding motion along the surface.

cards.front: For a simple ramp, what is gravity’s component down the slope?
cards.back: m g sin θ, parallel to the ramp.

cards.front: For a simple ramp, what is gravity’s component into the slope?
cards.back: m g cos θ, perpendicular to the ramp.

cards.front: When does a ramp have N = mg cos θ?
cards.back: When no other perpendicular forces act and normal acceleration is zero.

cards.front: If an applied force points θ above horizontal, what is F_x?
cards.back: F_x = F cos θ.

cards.front: If an applied force points θ above horizontal, what is F_y?
cards.back: F_y = F sin θ.

cards.front: How do you begin a free-body diagram?
cards.back: Isolate one object and draw only actual external forces on it.

cards.front: What is tension T in a rope?
cards.back: A pulling force transmitted by the rope, measured in newtons (N).

cards.front: What are ideal Atwood-machine assumptions?
cards.back: Massless rope and pulley, negligible friction, consistent acceleration.

cards.front: How is ideal Atwood acceleration found?
cards.back: a = (m_heavy − m_light)g/(m_heavy + m_light).

cards.front: In an elevator moving upward with acceleration, how is N related to mg?
cards.back: N − mg = ma with upward chosen positive.

cards.front: What does a bathroom scale measure in an elevator?
cards.back: Normal force (apparent weight), not mass directly.

cards.front: What does the symbol g mean, and what value should you learn?
cards.back: g = downward gravitational acceleration ≈ 9.8 m/s² near Earth’s surface. It is an approximation.

cards.front: When would you NOT use 9.8 m/s² for g?
cards.back: When the problem supplies a different g or the near-Earth surface approximation is not appropriate.

cards.front: What is the exact definition of 1 newton (N)?
cards.back: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². Force has units of mass × acceleration.

cards.front: A box has known net force Fnet and mass m. Find acceleration a. Formula?
cards.back: a = Fnet/m. Fnet in N; m in kg; a in m/s².

cards.front: A box has known mass m and acceleration a. Find net force Fnet. Formula?
cards.back: Fnet = ma. m in kg; a in m/s²; Fnet in N.

cards.front: Given mass m and gravity g, how do you calculate weight W?
cards.back: W = mg. m in kg, g ≈ 9.8 m/s² near Earth; W is downward force in N.

cards.front: A box rests on a level floor with no vertical acceleration. What is N?
cards.back: N = mg if only weight and floor normal force act vertically. N is normal force (newtons).

cards.front: A box slides across a surface and μₖ and N are given. Find friction?
cards.back: fₖ = μₖN; fₖ is kinetic friction (N), μₖ unitless friction coefficient, N normal force (N).

cards.front: An object slides down a frictionless inclined plane. Find acceleration?
cards.back: a = g sinθ down the ramp, assuming no other parallel force. θ is slope angle; g is gravitational acceleration.

cards.front: For a ramp with angle θ, which gravity component pulls down the ramp?
cards.back: F_parallel = mg sinθ; m mass (kg), g gravity (m/s²), θ ramp angle.

cards.front: For a simple ramp, which gravity component pushes into the ramp?
cards.back: F_perp = mg cosθ; normal force N equals this only if no other perpendicular forces/acceleration.

cards.front: A pull force F makes angle θ above horizontal. Which components?
cards.back: Fₓ = F cosθ (horizontal); Fᵧ = F sinθ (upward), for θ measured above horizontal.

cards.front: A pull points upward at an angle on a level floor. How is N found?
cards.back: N = mg − F sinθ if vertical acceleration is zero and only weight, normal and upward pull act vertically.

cards.front: A push points downward at an angle on a level floor. How is N found?
cards.back: N = mg + F sinθ if vertical acceleration is zero and only weight, normal and downward push act vertically.

cards.front: Two hanging masses over an ideal pulley move together. Find acceleration?
cards.back: a = (m_heavy − m_light)g/(m_heavy + m_light); ideal rope and pulley, negligible friction.

cards.front: A pulley problem asks how far a mass falls after t seconds. What sequence?
cards.back: First find a with ΣF = ma for the system, then use Δx = v_i t + ½at² if a is constant.

cards.front: An elevator accelerates upward. Find scale reading N. Which equation?
cards.back: N = m(g+a), with upward-positive acceleration a. N is apparent weight in newtons.

cards.front: An elevator accelerates downward. Find scale reading N. Which equation?
cards.back: N = m(g−a_down) if a_down is the positive magnitude of downward acceleration.

cards.front: An elevator moves at constant speed. How does scale reading compare to mg?
cards.back: N = mg when acceleration is zero and the only vertical forces are normal and gravity.

cards.front: A box is at rest. What must net force and acceleration be?
cards.back: ΣF = 0 N and a = 0 m/s². All force components balance.

cards.front: What does voltage measure?
cards.back: Electric potential difference, measured in volts (V).

cards.front: What is current I?
cards.back: Electric charge flow per second, measured in amperes (A).

cards.front: What is resistance R?
cards.back: Opposition to electric current, measured in ohms (Ω).

cards.front: What is electrical power P?
cards.back: Energy transferred per second, measured in watts (W).

cards.front: What does Ohm’s law state?
cards.back: V = IR for an ohmic component under applicable conditions.

cards.front: How can current be calculated from voltage and resistance?
cards.back: I = V/R.

cards.front: How can resistance be calculated from voltage and current?
cards.back: R = V/I, for nonzero current.

cards.front: How is electrical power calculated from voltage and current?
cards.back: P = IV.

cards.front: How does current behave in a series circuit?
cards.back: The same current flows through each component.

cards.front: How does voltage behave in parallel branches?
cards.back: Each branch across the same two nodes has the same voltage.

cards.front: What is total resistance in series?
cards.back: R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + … .

cards.front: How is equivalent parallel resistance calculated?
How should a series-parallel combination be simplified?
cards.back: Combine obvious series or parallel groups step by step.

cards.front: What is the voltage-sum check in a simple closed circuit loop?
cards.back: The sum of voltage drops equals the applied source voltage.

cards.front: What is the current-sum check at a junction?
cards.back: Total current entering equals total current leaving.

cards.front: Why is parallel equivalent resistance below the smallest branch resistance?
cards.back: Adding branches creates more current paths for the same voltage.

cards.front: What is the exact definition of 1 ohm (Ω)?
cards.back: 1 Ω = 1 V/A: one volt of potential difference per ampere of current.

cards.front: Given voltage V and resistance R, find current I. Formula?
cards.back: I = V/R. V in volts, R in ohms, I in amperes (Ohm’s law).

cards.front: An electrical problem gives I and R, asks voltage. Which equation?
cards.back: V = IR; V: voltage (V), I: current (A), R: resistance (Ω), for an ohmic element.

cards.front: An electrical problem gives V and I, asks resistance. Which equation?
cards.back: R = V/I, I ≠ 0; V voltage (V), I current (A), R resistance (Ω), for an ohmic element.

cards.front: Given voltage V and current I, find electrical power P. Formula?
cards.back: P = IV. P in watts; V in volts; I in amperes.

cards.front: A circuit gives current and resistance; asks power. Which formula?
cards.back: P = I²R; P: power (W), I: current (A), R: resistance (Ω), for an ohmic resistor.

cards.front: A circuit gives voltage and resistance; asks power. Which formula?
cards.back: P = V²/R; P: power (W), V: voltage (V), R: resistance (Ω), for an ohmic resistor.

cards.front: One continuous path through resistors: series or parallel?
cards.back: Series. Current I is the same through each resistor; resistances add.

cards.front: Multiple resistor branches share the same two endpoints: series or parallel?
cards.back: Parallel. Voltage V is the same across every branch; branch currents add.

cards.front: Find equivalent resistance of series resistors. Which formula?
cards.back: R_eq = R₁+R₂+...; sum all resistor values in ohms (Ω).

cards.front: Find equivalent resistance of parallel resistors. Which formula?
cards.back: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁+1/R₂+...; R values are in ohms (Ω).

cards.front: Only two resistors are in parallel. What shortcut can find R_eq?
cards.back: R_eq = (R₁R₂)/(R₁+R₂); both resistances R₁ and R₂ are in ohms.

cards.front: A combination circuit has a small series pair inside a larger network. First step?
cards.back: Reduce the clearly series/parallel subgroup, redraw the simplified circuit, and repeat.

cards.front: At a circuit junction, which law checks the currents?
cards.back: Current entering = current leaving (Kirchhoff current rule).

cards.front: Around a closed circuit loop, which law checks voltages?
cards.back: The signed voltage changes sum to zero (Kirchhoff voltage rule).

cards.front: A 12 V battery feeds three resistors in series. What is fixed across them?
cards.back: The current is identical through all three; their individual voltage drops add to 12 V.

cards.front: A 12 V source feeds two parallel branches. What is fixed across both?
cards.back: Each branch has 12 V across it if both connect to the same two ideal source nodes.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.1: Convert 768 miles/hour to meters/second.
Worksheet 2.2: 340 miles on 13.2 gallons. Find miles per gallon.
cards.back:
≈26 mpg; 25.8 mpg if 340 miles is treated as 3 significant figures.
mpg = total miles ÷ gallons.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.3: Moon is 384,403 km away; quarter diameter 2.3 cm. How many quarters?
cards.back:
≈ 1.7 × 10¹⁰ quarters
Convert km→cm, then divide by 2.3 cm per quarter.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.4: Convert 3,106 carats to mg; 1 carat = 0.2 g.
cards.back:
621,200 mg using exact metric carat conversion; the given 0.2 can imply coarser reported precision.
carats × (0.2 g/carat) × (1000 mg/g).

cards.front: Worksheet 2.5: 60 heartbeats/min over 79 years. Estimate total beats in scientific notation.
cards.back:
≈ 2.5 × 10⁹ beats
beats/min × 60 min/h × 24 h/day × 365 days/yr × 79 yr.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.6: Convert 175 km/h to miles/hour.
cards.back:
≈ 109 mph
km/h ÷ 1.609344 km/mile.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.7: A cliff is 150 m away. Echo return time? Assume sound speed 343 m/s.
cards.back:
≈0.87 s if air sound speed is assumed to be 343 m/s (not specified in original question).
t = 2d/vsound; echo makes a 300 m round trip.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.8: Chairlift: 4,806 ft in 9 min. Find speed in mph and ft/s.
cards.back:
6.07 mph; 8.90 ft/s
speed = distance ÷ time; use 60 s/min and 5280 ft/mile.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.9: Convert 2.98 m² to cm².
cards.back:
2.98 × 10⁴ cm²
Use (100 cm/m)², not 100.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.10: Convert 3,600 in² to ft² (1 ft = 12 in).
cards.back:
25 ft²
Divide by (12 in/ft)² = 144.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.11: Convert 4.5 km² to m².
cards.back:
4.5 × 10⁶ m²
Multiply by (1000 m/km)².

cards.front: Worksheet 2.12: Convert 350 in³ to cm³ (1 in = 2.54 cm).
cards.back:
≈ 5.74 × 10³ cm³
Multiply by (2.54 cm/in)³.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.13: Tank is 60 × 30 × 40 cm. Find volume in cm³, m³, and liters.
cards.back:
72,000 cm³ = 0.072 m³ = 72 L
V = length × width × height.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.14: Convert 450 m³ of pool water to liters.
Worksheet 2.15: Convert density 7.87 g/cm³ to kg/m³.
cards.back:
7.87 × 10³ kg/m³
Convert g→kg and cm³→m³ separately.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.16: Convert g = 9.8 m/s² to ft/s² (1 m = 3.28 ft).
cards.back:
≈ 32 ft/s²
9.8 m/s² × 3.28 ft/m.

cards.front: Worksheet 2.17: Convert acceleration 3.5 m/s² to km/h².
cards.back:
≈ 4.5 × 10⁴ km/h²
Multiply by (1 km/1000 m) × (3600 s/h)².

cards.front: Worksheet 3.1: Walk 3.0 km east and 4.0 km north. Displacement magnitude?
cards.back:
5.0 km
R=√(x²+y²).

cards.front: Worksheet 3.2: Boat velocity 4.0 m/s across, current 3.0 m/s downstream. Resultant speed?
cards.back:
5.0 m/s
R=√(vx²+vy²).

cards.front: Worksheet 3.3: Run 12 m west then 9.0 m south. Straight-line displacement?
cards.back:
15 m
R=√(x²+y²).

cards.front: Worksheet 3.4: Vector x = +6.0 m, y = −8.0 m. Find its magnitude.
cards.back:
10 m
R=√(x²+y²).

cards.front: Worksheet 3.5: A 12 m ladder is 65° above ground. Find height and distance from wall.
cards.back:
Height ≈ 10.9 m; base ≈ 5.07 m
height=Lsinθ; base=Lcosθ.

cards.front: Worksheet 3.6: A 60 m kite string is 40° above ground. Find kite height.
cards.back:
≈ 38.6 m
height=Lsinθ.

cards.front: Worksheet 3.7: Kick at 18 m/s, 35° above horizontal. Find vx and vy.
cards.back:
vₓ ≈ 14.7 m/s; vᵧ ≈ 10.3 m/s
vx=vcosθ; vy=vsinθ.

cards.front: Worksheet 3.8: Plane flies 250 m/s, 30° north of east. Find east and north velocity.
cards.back:
East ≈ 217 m/s; north = 125 m/s
vx=vcosθ; vy=vsinθ.

cards.front: Worksheet 3.9: Ramp length 5.0 m, rise 0.40 m. Find incline angle.
cards.back:
≈ 4.6°
θ=sin⁻¹(rise/hypotenuse).

cards.front: Worksheet 3.10: Walk 3.0 km east then 4.0 km north. Magnitude and angle north of east?
cards.back:
5.0 km at 53.1° north of east
R=√(x²+y²); θ=tan⁻¹(y/x).

cards.front: Worksheet 3.11: Dog pulled 15 N east and 20 N north. Resultant force and direction?
cards.back:
25 N at 53.1° north of east
R=√(Fx²+Fy²); θ=tan⁻¹(Fy/Fx).

cards.front: Worksheet 3.12: Drive 25 km at 30° north of east, then 40 km north. Resultant displacement?
cards.back:
≈ 56.8 km at 67.6° north of east
Resolve both vectors into x and y; add; calculate R and θ.

cards.front: Worksheet 3.13: Add vector A = 10 m at 0° and B = 15 m at 120°. Find magnitude/direction.
cards.back:
≈ 13.2 m at 79.1° counterclockwise from east
Ax=10; Bx=15cos120°; By=15sin120°; then R and θ.

cards.front: Worksheet 4.1: Ball launched horizontally at 5.6 m/s from 85 m. Flight time, range, impact velocity?
cards.back:
(a) 4.16 s; (b) 23.3 m; (c) 41.2 m/s at 82.2° below horizontal.
t=√(2h/g); range=vxt; vy=−gt; |v|=√(vx²+vy²).

cards.front: Worksheet 4.2: Launch 200 m/s at 47°; same landing height. Time, height, range, velocity at 5 s?
cards.back:
(a) 29.9 s; (b) 1.09×10³ m; (c) 4.07×10³ m; (d) 168 m/s at 35.5° above horizontal.
v0x=v0cosθ; v0y=v0sinθ; tflight=2v0y/g (same height).

cards.front: Worksheet 4.3: Launch 65 m/s at 37° from 125 m cliff. Time, max height, range, impact velocity?
cards.back:
(a) 10.43 s; (b) 203 m above ground; (c) 541 m; (d) 81.7 m/s, 50.6° below horizontal.
Δy=v0yt−½gt²; use −125 m landing displacement.

cards.front: Worksheet 4.4: Ball launched horizontally at 4.8 m/s from 50 m. Time, range, impact velocity?
cards.back:
(a) 3.19 s; (b) 15.3 m; (c) 31.7 m/s at 81.3° below horizontal
t=√(2h/g); range=vxt; vy=−gt.

cards.front: Worksheet 4.5: Starts from rest; constant a = 8.4 m/s² for 11 s. Final velocity?
cards.back:
92.4 m/s (≈ 92 m/s to two sig figs)
vf=vi+at, with vi=0.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.1: A 10 kg cat rests on a flat frictionless stool. Normal force and net force?
cards.back:
N = 98 N up; net force = 0 N
N=mg at rest on a horizontal stool; ΣF=0.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.2: A 12 kg apple rests on a flat frictionless bench. Normal and net force?
cards.back:
N = 117.6 N; net force = 0 N
N=mg at rest on a horizontal bench; ΣF=0.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.3: 5 kg box slides down 50° ramp; μk=0.30. Net force and acceleration?
cards.back:
Fnet ≈ 28.09 N downhill; a ≈ 5.617 m/s² downhill
Fnet=mg(sinθ−μk cosθ); a=Fnet/m.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.4: 15 kg box slides down 40° ramp; μk=0.764. Net force and acceleration?
cards.back:
Fnet ≈ 8.46 N downhill; a ≈ 0.564 m/s² downhill
Fnet=mg(sinθ−μk cosθ); a=Fnet/m.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.5: 51 kg box slides down 80° ramp; μk=0.21. Net force and acceleration?
cards.back:
Fnet ≈ 473.98 N downhill; a ≈ 9.294 m/s² downhill
Fnet=mg(sinθ−μk cosθ); a=Fnet/m.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.6: 20 kg sled, frictionless, pulled 80 N at 30° upward. Normal force and acceleration?
cards.back:
N = 156 N; a ≈ 3.46 m/s² forward
N=mg−Tsinθ; a=Tcosθ/m.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.7: 15 kg box pulled 60 N at 25° upward, μk=0.20. Normal, friction, acceleration?
cards.back:
N ≈ 122 N; friction ≈ 24.3 N; a ≈ 2.00 m/s²
N=mg−Fsinθ; fk=μkN; a=(Fcosθ−fk)/m.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.8: 18 kg mower pushed 120 N at 40° downward, μk=0.35. Normal and acceleration?
cards.back:
N ≈ 254 N; a ≈ 0.177 m/s² forward
N=mg+Fsinθ; fk=μkN; a=(Fcosθ−fk)/m.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.9: 25 kg suitcase pulled at 35° upward, μk=0.30, constant velocity. Tension?
cards.back:
T ≈ 74.2 N
Constant velocity ⇒ horizontal net force 0; Tcosθ=μk(mg−Tsinθ).

cards.front: Worksheet 5.10: Ideal Atwood: 3.0 kg and 5.0 kg hanging. Acceleration and tension?
cards.back:
a = 2.45 m/s² (5 kg down); T = 36.75 N
a=(mheavy−mlight)g/(mheavy+mlight); T from either mass.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.11: Ideal Atwood: 10 kg and 12 kg, start at rest. a, tension, fall in 2.0 s?
cards.back:
a ≈ 0.891 m/s²; T ≈ 107 N; fall ≈ 1.78 m
a=(mheavy−mlight)g/mtotal; s=½at² from rest.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.12: Ideal Atwood: 4.0 kg moves up at 2.0 m/s². Find other mass.
cards.back:
M ≈ 6.05 kg
Use ideal Atwood acceleration and solve for unknown mass.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.13: 4 kg block on frictionless table + hanging 2 kg mass. a and rope tension?
cards.back:
a ≈ 3.27 m/s²; T ≈ 13.1 N
a=mhang g/(mtable+mhang), T=mtable a.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.14: Same as 5.13, but table friction μk=0.25. a and rope tension?
cards.back:
a ≈ 1.63 m/s²; T ≈ 16.3 N
a=(mhang g−μk mtable g)/(mtable+mhang).

cards.front: Worksheet 5.15: 6 kg block on 30° frictionless ramp, hanging 5 kg. Motion, a, tension?
cards.back:
5 kg falls, 6 kg moves up slope; a≈1.78 m/s²; T≈40.1 N.
Compare mhang g with mramp gsinθ; ΣF=ma.

cards.front: Worksheet 5.16: 70 kg person in elevator; at rest, accelerating ±2.0 m/s². Scale readings?
cards.back:
(a) 686 N; (b) 826 N; (c) 546 N
N=m(g+a) for up acceleration; N=m(g−a) for down magnitude.

cards.front: Worksheet 6.1: 9.0 V across 450 Ω. Current?
Worksheet 6.2: 0.25 A through 120 Ω. Voltage?
cards.back:
30 V
V=IR.

cards.front: Worksheet 6.3: 120 V draws 2.5 A. Resistance?
cards.back:
48 Ω
R=V/I.

cards.front: Worksheet 6.4: 60 W bulb on 120 V. Current and resistance?
cards.back:
I = 0.50 A; R = 240 Ω
I=P/V; R=V²/P.

cards.front: Worksheet 6.5: 1500 W dryer at 120 V. Current?
Worksheet 6.6: 10Ω, 20Ω, 30Ω in series at 12V. Total R, I, each voltage drop?
cards.back:
Rtotal=60 Ω; I=0.20 A; drops=2 V, 4 V, 6 V
Req=sum R; I=V/Req; voltage drops=IR.

cards.front: Worksheet 6.7: Two series bulbs. What happens to the other if one burns out?
cards.back:
The other bulb goes out too.
Series has one path; a burnt bulb opens the loop.

cards.front: Worksheet 6.8: 6Ω, 12Ω, 4Ω in parallel at 24V. Total R, branch currents, total I?
cards.back:
Rtotal=2 Ω; branch currents=4 A, 2 A, 6 A; total=12 A
1/Req=sum(1/Ri); each branch I=V/Ri.

cards.front: Worksheet 6.9: Why are household outlets connected in parallel?
cards.back:
Parallel provides independent operation at the intended supply voltage.
Parallel branches each receive source voltage and operate independently.

cards.front: Worksheet 6.10: 4Ω series with (6Ω || 3Ω) at 18V. Total R, I, two voltage drops?
cards.back:
Rtotal=6 Ω; Itotal=3 A; V₄=12 V; Vparallel=6 V
Parallel 6||3 = 2Ω; add series 4Ω; use V=IR.

cards.front: Worksheet 6.11: (10Ω || 10Ω) series 15Ω at 12V. Total R, total I, branch currents?
cards.back:
Rtotal=20 Ω; Itotal=0.60 A; current in each 10Ω=0.30 A
Parallel 10||10 = 5Ω; +15Ω series; branch currents split equally.

cards.front: Worksheet 6.12: Sketch a battery and switch with two lamps in parallel. How are they wired?
cards.back:
Diagram: battery (+) — switch — A — [lamp 1 ∥ lamp 2] — B — battery (−)
Both bulbs connect between the same two junctions after the switch.
